idiom_name: `clone(): this` using the polymorphic `this` type, with a hand-written body per class; `structuredClone` for data-only graphs
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds the typing half of the virtual constructor: declaring `clone(): this` on a base class or interface uses the polymorphic `this` type (F-bounded polymorphism), so every override promises the caller's own subtype - code that clones a `Circle` is typed `Circle` without a cast, which is the type-level counterpart of a covariant return. The runtime is still JavaScript, so the body is a hand-written method (often `Object.assign(Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(this)), this)` plus per-class fixes), and `structuredClone` remains the deep-copy tool for plain data - it does not preserve prototypes and so cannot satisfy `clone(): this` for class instances. There is a known soundness hole to know about: a `this`-returning method must return the receiver, so a cloning implementation that builds a new instance needs a cast, and subclasses that do not override an inherited `this`-typed clone get a method that lies about its type (long-standing issue #283).
pitfalls: `clone(): this` must be implemented with a cast (`return new Circle(this.r) as this`), because TypeScript requires a `this`-returning method to return the receiver; a subclass that inherits an unoverridden `this`-typed clone therefore claims a type it does not produce.

An interface can declare the contract (`interface Shape { clone(): this }`) but never the behaviour - every implementer still writes the body, and TypeScript cannot check that the returned object is a fresh, independent instance.

`structuredClone` is typed but unsound for the pattern: it throws for functions and drops prototypes, accessors and private fields, so it cannot be used to satisfy a `clone(): this` signature and should be reserved for data-only graphs.
